blocks.text: High-level policy should not depend on low-level details. Both should depend on abstractions that the policy owns.

The inversion has two parts. Source dependencies point at an **abstraction**, and that abstraction is **owned by the consumer**: `OrderService` defines `Notifier` in terms of what orders need, and SMTP adapts to it. That is what lets the business core build and test without infrastructure.

items: **Not the same as DI:** DIP is the design rule; injection is one way to satisfy it.
**Ownership matters:** an interface that mirrors the vendor API is not inversion.
**Boundary:** invert at module and layer seams, not around every `new`.

blocks.text: `new ArrayList<>()` in a method does not violate DIP. Depending on a slow, external or unstable detail does.

cards.expectedOutput:
SMTP ada
SMTP ada: Order confirmed
test double saw [grace/Order confirmed]

walkthrough.note: The high-level `OrderServiceBefore` constructs `SmtpClient` itself. Policy now depends on a detail and cannot run without it.
The abstraction is shaped by what orders need to say, not by SMTP. It lives with the high-level code.
`OrderService` depends only on `Notifier`. Its source no longer mentions SMTP, so it compiles and tests without infrastructure.
The details now point inward: both the SMTP adapter and a recording test double implement the abstraction.
Composition happens at the edge. Production passes the SMTP notifier; a test passes the recorder and asserts on what it saw.

blocks.text: A trading engine that must run live and in backtests.

A strategy engine called a vendor's WebSocket client directly, so strategies could only be tested against the live market. The core now declares `MarketData` with the two operations it needs. A `VendorFeed` adapter implements it in production and a `CsvReplay` in backtests. The same engine produces both results, and switching vendors touches one adapter.
Payoff: backtests are deterministic, and a vendor change never reaches the trading logic.

lists.title: Use when
items: Core logic must be tested without network, disk or clock.
An infrastructure choice such as vendor or database may change.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: The dependency is a stable platform type such as `String`, `List` or `Instant`.
The script is tiny and wiring costs more than the coupling.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: An interface shaped like the vendor API leaks the detail it should hide.
Placing the abstraction in the infrastructure module: the arrow does not invert.
A Service Locator hides dependencies instead of inverting them.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: Mocking every collaborator so tests restate the implementation.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Constructor injection with `final` fields satisfies DIP with no container.
JPMS `provides ... with` lets a module supply an implementation of another module's service.

rows.difference: DIP says who owns the abstraction; injection is the mechanism that hands the implementation in.
A locator also decouples from the concrete class but hides dependencies inside method bodies and makes them harder to see and test.
Ports and adapters is DIP applied to a whole architecture: the domain owns the ports, infrastructure adapts.
The low-level detail is usually wrapped in an adapter that implements the high-level abstraction.
Programming to an interface is the local habit; DIP adds that the consumer owns the interface and the arrow flips.

entries.name: java.sql.Connection and javax.sql.DataSource
entries.detail: Application code depends on the JDBC abstraction; each vendor driver implements it.

entries.name: org.slf4j.Logger
entries.detail: Libraries log through the facade; Logback or Log4j 2 bind behind it.

entries.name: jakarta.persistence.EntityManager
entries.detail: Business code uses the API; Hibernate or EclipseLink implement it as the provider.

entries.name: Constructor injection in the ApplicationContext
entries.detail: Beans declare abstractions they need; the container supplies implementations.

exercises.prompt: Which principle does this class most clearly violate?
lines: private final PostgresClient db = new PostgresClient("prod-db:5432");
private final SmtpClient mail = new SmtpClient("smtp.corp");

options.why: The high-level job constructs and depends on concrete infrastructure instead of abstractions it owns.
Adding behavior is not the issue; the issue is hard-wired details.
The job has one purpose; the problem is who it constructs, not what it does.
There are no interfaces here at all, so none can be too wide.

template: class PostgresClient { PostgresClient(String h) {} String query(String q) { return ""; } }
class SmtpClient { SmtpClient(String h) {} void send(String to, String b) {} }

exercises.scenario: Your domain module imports `com.vendor.s3.S3Client` and calls it directly in 60 classes. Switching to another object store next year would touch all of them, and unit tests need a MinIO container.
exercises.prompt: Which principle should guide the redesign?

options.why: Define a `BlobStore` abstraction in the domain module and make the S3 code implement it, so the domain no longer knows the vendor.
Extension points would not remove the vendor import from the domain.
Splitting classes would not change what they depend on.
The coupling is to a concrete service, not to a parent class.

exercises.prompt: Tap the line that bypasses the injected abstraction.
lines: interface Mailer { void send(String to, String body); }
exercises.explanation: The service takes a `Mailer` but ignores it and builds a concrete `SmtpMailer`, so it stays coupled to SMTP and cannot be tested in isolation. Use the injected `mailer`.

template: class SmtpMailer implements Mailer { SmtpMailer(String host) {} public void send(String t, String b) {} }

exercises.prompt: Order the test so that each line only uses what came before.
exercises.explanation: Create the test double, inject it, trigger the behavior, then inspect what the double recorded.

template: interface Notifier { void notify(String c, String m); }
final class RecordingNotifier implements Notifier { final List<String> sent = new ArrayList<>(); public void notify(String c, String m) { sent.add(c); } }
final class OrderService { OrderService(Notifier n) {} void place(String c) {} }

exercises.prompt: Explain the Dependency Inversion Principle in your own words. What is inverted, and how is it different from dependency injection?

modelAnswer.text: High-level policy and low-level details both depend on an abstraction, and the policy owns that abstraction, so source dependencies point toward the business core instead of away from it. Dependency injection is only a mechanism for supplying the implementation; DIP is the rule about direction and ownership.

keyPoints: Both sides depend on an abstraction
DI is a mechanism, not the principle
Invert at seams, not around every new
